[ 3m15s948ms - 3m21s708ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights "This episode is for you."

[ 4m48s778ms - 4m56s148ms ] The screen returns to the web page. He highlights the text, "I generally just talk to the model a couple of times to start feeding in context about what I'm trying to do, then I'll switch into spec mode to start getting a plan going on what I wanna build."
[ 4m56s148ms - 5m5s878ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "In spec mode I'll basically question a bunch of things. Like I don't understand what this is, or why would we need that over this, can't we do it this way?"
[ 5m5s878ms - 5m17s338ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "I'll link docs and GitHub repos for the agent to explore."
[ 5m17s338ms - 5m32s838ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Then I let Opus 4.5 with autonomy high just rip. [ 5m32s838ms - 5m37s458ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "I start the server, test it, give feedback and iterate."
[ 5m37s458ms - 6m4s468ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "So I kind of build ahead of myself first. I try and just build the thing. [ 6m4s468ms - 6m12s868ms ] The screen cuts to an image of a web page titled "AGENTS.md" with text that reads, "A simple, open format for guiding coding agents, used by over 60K open-source projects." The man speaks in the corner of the screen.
[ 6m12s868ms - 6m25s798ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Think of AGENTS.md as a README for agents: a dedicated, predictable place to provide the context and instructions to help coding agents work on your project."
[ 6m25s798ms - 6m43s558ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Why AGENTS.md?" and a list of reasons. He then highlights example commands.
[ 6m43s558ms - 7m15s88ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "My agents.md setup" and explains his setup. In that repos folder is an agents.md that says to explicitly set up each new repo with what to do and not to do, how to do things with GitHub, how to commit, all that kind of stuff. [ 7m15s88ms - 7m33s848ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Running tests. End-to-end tests is one of these things I never really paid attention to previously. But now I'm really keen to have end-to-end tests on everything. Given my current knowledge and capability, when I'm building things and testing them, there often might be silly bugs that I just should have caught or tested had there been tests in the first place."
[ 7m33s848ms - 7m48s948ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "And I often look at others' agents.md files to see what I can borrow for my own. I'm constantly trying to improve my doc to make each and every new working session smoother."

[ 8m16s388ms - 8m31s388ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "It lets me code from my phone, and add new things when I'm out and about. That in combination with my Telegram bot makes it really easy for me to do things when I'm not at my desk."
[ 8m31s388ms - 8m59s38ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "I also use Slack with my agent. [ 8m59s38ms - 9m44s798ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "What I've been learning" and then "Bash commands." [ 9m44s798ms - 10m12s868ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "From there I started getting more into bash + cli's. So with Supabase, Vercel and Github, I'm always using the CLI's over the MCP's."
[ 10m12s868ms - 10m45s398ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "I often build my own CLIs for things. [ 10m45s398ms - 11m47s488ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "VPS". I abstractly knew what it was—it's like another computer that is on all the time somewhere else. But until I truly needed one I didn't really know what I needed to do there, and there's still a lot I need to learn. But effectively, now when I'm running the crypto tracker, I have a ton of data that's being pulled every single minute and I need that to always stay on."
[ 11m47s488ms - 11m52s898ms ] The man performs a Google search for "vps".
[ 11m52s898ms - 11m56s658ms ] The screen displays Google search results for "vps", including images and definitions.
[ 11m56s658ms - 12m4s18ms ] The screen returns to the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "I also use the VPS when using my Droid Telegram bot and use something called SyncThing to sync my local repos to my VPS so that my repos are always up to date and they're in the same state as I left it. So I can just pick it up on the go."
[ 12m4s18ms - 12m24s848ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Skills". I've tried to use them a bit more. I've been using them not only just as knowledge, but also with bash commands + CLIs. I've got a Gmail CLI that I can pull into any projects, it's portable, it lives at my root directory. So anytime I need Gmail in my system—I've got a Gmail triage system that I use—it just uses the CLI."
[ 12m24s848ms - 12m39s488ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "The new programmable layer of abstraction" and then a quote, "Not to be like everyone else on Twitter when they see Andrej Karpathy tweeting something, but this really rang true to me: 'there's a new programmable layer of abstraction to master'."
[ 12m39s488ms - 12m56s88ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "When it was the no-code days, the abstraction layer that I was mastering was drag and drop tools like Webflow, Zapier, and Airtable—stitching them together and making it feel like real software (until you hit a limit)."
[ 12m56s88ms - 13m20s598ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "But now instead of me thinking I've got to learn to write code from scratch in order to be able to do all of this, what I need to learn is actually **how to work with an AI agent.** How can I prompt it well? How can I make sure it's got the right context? And also how can it help me understand what we're doing, how do the pieces work together, how can I improve my own system over time?"
[ 13m20s598ms - 13m25s938ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Including all of the things like agents, subagents, prompts, context, memory, skills, hooks, etc."
[ 13m25s938ms - 13m56s268ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Learning from others" and then "I read people like Peter Steinberger who is an 'actual' programmer and is shipping a ton like crazy. And seeing in his posts almost the simplicity of his system, where he just talks to the model, lets it do its thing, doesn't really worry about extra slash commands, subagents, hooks, skills(although he's coming round to skills) - this just gives me permission and confidence that I don't need some ultra complex system."
[ 13m56s268ms - 14m31s388ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Looking at Twitter you see a lot of people really optimising or potentially over-optimising their own system. That can feel daunting for folks like me, but also that's what I think some of the beauty of this is: It's a completely customizable system, so you can make it work for you however you'd like it to work. You can have a plan mode that you create with a custom slash command that runs for twenty minutes like Kieran does, or you can just talk to the model like Peter does."
[ 14m31s388ms - 14m54s748ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Another thing while following other engineers is seeing their open source software, cloning it, using it myself, trying to improve it, or just taking parts of it and making that my own. Like Peter's recent summarize Youtube for example. I just took it, removed the Chrome extension part, kept it as the CLI, and now I can just talk to that anywhere I want to."
[ 14m54s748ms - 15m5s88ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "And like Mario, reading things like his MCP post where he talks about CLIs over MCPs, gave me the nudge to dive in more to bash and CLIs."
[ 15m5s88ms - 15m31s638ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "The learning process" and then "I'm not building things for tens of thousands of people to use in production. So there are going to be bugs, there are gonna be issues, and I run into them plenty. And it's just a reminder that this is a gap in your knowledge, not in the capability that you have now."
[ 15m31s638ms - 15m45s368ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "My role is identifying the gaps or finding those gaps and thinking: how do I make sure this never happens again? Or how do I make sure I understand this part of the system enough that if it's gonna happen again, I'll catch it."
[ 15m45s368ms - 16m9s328ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Even the simplest things from when I first started using agents to code—like, why can't I use GitHub Pages when I've got dynamic data and I want multiple users to be able to use something? That's a very, very simple thing that programmers know. But it was something I just learned because I was building something, I was trying to build something different than the tools allowed me."
[ 16m9s328ms - 16m45s28ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "So then I said, okay, so what do we need to do? Like all you need to do is just ask the model. The model knows everything that you don't. You can just keep asking it. "It's your ever patient, over-your-shoulder, expert programmer." You can add in your agents.md "I am not a programmer, you need to explain things very simply for me." You can just tweak it exactly how you want to."
[ 16m45s28ms - 17m4s968ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Contributing to real products" and then "I've even contributed improvements to our own product—some simple things, but improvements nonetheless. There's a team of engineers at Factory that are extremely experienced and good at what they do, and I'm learning a lot by just watching them, looking at their PRs. We have internal lunch and learns where people say "this is how I scope new product features", "here's how I bug fix", things like that, which have been really helpful."
[ 17m4s968ms - 18m5s88ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "So this whole thing is just a really big learning experience for me, and I'm really enjoying learning "to code", or, learning to work with code."
[ 18m5s88ms - 18m22s758ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Why this is different" and then "I've tried to learn to code many times in my life, and every time it was type in these characters, hit enter, and do you see hello world? It was kind of do this, then that, then this happens. And maybe it would have been helpful for me to learn all that, but I just still think that's so different to what it is today."
[ 18m22s758ms - 18m42s688ms ] The man performs a Google search for "hello world print screen". The search results show images of various "hello world" programs in different programming languages.
[ 18m42s688ms - 19m5s48ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "For me to be able to build the things I've built now, if I'd taken that other path, I would have had to code for many months, many years to get to a point where I could feel like I could write the code myself."
[ 19m5s48ms - 19m31s528ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "So instead I'm coming at it from a point of view of I understand systems thinking for projects built with code. I accidentally learned that when I was running my last company with no-code education. You're still learning that okay. Webflow is the front end, Zapier is the API routes, the connective tissue, the data flows, and Airtable is your database. So I learned the systems of that previously, and I think that's helping me today understand some of those pieces."
[ 19m31s528ms - 19m57s328ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "There is so much you can learn. And often I'll see something that someone posts on Twitter and I'm like, I have no idea what that is or what I can do with it, but I'll bet you I can play around with it."
[ 19m57s328ms - 20m23s808ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "No piece of software feels unattainable. "I can just git clone it and say, what the hell does this thing do? Okay, I've been thinking about this—is this thing gonna do anything related to what I thought? And it's just all exploration. It's so much fun."
[ 20m23s808ms - 20m38s998ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Asking the "silly" questions" and then "There have been countless times where I think about silly questions—to me or silly questions that other programmers would never ask—that I have the permission to ask, because there's no one watching me and no one shooting me down for being stupid or saying the wrong thing."
[ 20m38s998ms - 21m17s128ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Like, why do we use all these frameworks, these different types of frameworks? Because they are abstractions for humans writing code. So why—if an LLM is super smart—why couldn't it just be simpler code written, less dependencies, less potential surface areas for bugs? Is that a silly thought or a good thought? And I can learn that it might not be a silly thought. But okay, yes, there are these many projects that the model has been trained on, which is why often things will be built in certain frameworks. So it's just building up this understanding of the code world, the engineering world that I didn't deserve to be in, but I'm absolutely part of now."
[ 21m17s128ms - 21m45s388ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Beyond "vibe coding"" and explains his perspective on "vibe coding" not being enough.
[ 21m45s388ms - 22m23s348ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "It feels like a game" and then "Some people have likened this new way of programming to a game. Factorio is the one that people talk about. I've never played it. I'm not much of a gamer. But this whole paradigm feels like a real game to me, and the output is I'm building stuff that I want to build. A ton of things just don't end up anywhere on Github. They don't end up live. They are just mere explorations of parts of a system or a topic. Others end up published and other people use it – I had a CTO fork my personal site and use it for himself! Big boss stuff (for me!)."
[ 22m23s348ms - 22m24s838ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Every idea you've ever had can be exercised, can be explored, and it doesn't need to be good" And you'll learn along the way.
[ 22m24s838ms - 22m42s918ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Permission to throw things away" and then "Previously, if I'd learnt to code to build a really crappy version of something I was thinking of, like a big idea that I had, and then no one wanted it, I'd be too emotionally invested in that idea to be able to just throw it away. With no-code, I could effectively build a version of that big idea in an hour, a couple of hours, a weekend. And if no one liked it, no one wanted to pay for it, it was rubbish, then I could just throw it away. It wasn't that much of my time or my energy into something that ultimately wasn't going to be something good for someone else."
[ 22m42s918ms - 23m4s788ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "And I feel like the same is true today. We're gonna see an explosion of software. Many of it won't be good, but lots of it is already great. There are expert programmers who are shipping things like absolute crazy that are all good projects. So we're just gonna have this absolute plethora of coded projects out there that you can use, clone, tweak, remix."
[ 23m4s788ms - 23m13s878ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "It'll take a lot less time than if you had to learn to code or if you're reading the files or you're writing the files or anything like that. It's just a lot quicker. The feedback loop is quicker. The process is quicker. You can just do anything at any time and just consistently keep churning out stuff."
[ 23m13s878ms - 23m15s948ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Fail forward" and then "The way to learn about code is to build ahead of your capability and fail forward."
[ 23m15s948ms - 23m29s888ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "I feel like everyone who is not technical today who wants to be in this world, who wants to do stuff like this, can absolutely do it. They just need some permission to do that. To play around. You must think of it like play."
[ 23m29s888ms - 23m44s878ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Sign up to a CLI agent like Droid. Say you want to build a personal website. Say you want to build a little RSS feed tracker, a little to-do list, a little workout app. Whatever you want to do, you just spin it up, start working on it. Every little hiccup, bug, or issue you run into—question it. Okay, why did this come up? Why did you hit those errors? You know you don't know how to code, so you shouldn't get bogged down with bugs—expert programmers hit bugs all the time."
[ 23m44s878ms - 23m55s278ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "And you can take it to other places. You can go to ChatGPT or Claude and give it to different models for different perspectives. You're always gonna have all of the choice up there and all the different variations."
[ 23m55s278ms - 24m2s98ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Just pick one" and then "There are just so many different tools, so many different options. Ultimately, just pick one and just stick with it. Just learn that system. They all look fairly similar. They all work similarly."
[ 24m2s98ms - 24m7s388ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Obviously, I use Droid because I work at Factory. But also they get the best output of any models. (yay for model agnostic)."
[ 24m7s388ms - 24m34s538ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Ultimately, what I want and what I need from a tool is: "Is this one gonna help me get the furthest I can in the least amount of time with the least amount of trouble?" The more I have to do with using the tools themselves, the harder it is."
[ 24m34s538ms - 24m53s538ms ] The screen displays the web page, with the man in the corner. He highlights the text, "Things like IDEs—I've tried a bunch. I used to use one in particular for a long time. It's just got so much extra stuff that I just don't need or care about. I just want to talk to a model, have code written. If I need to inspect some markdown files, I can now use what I've just recently discovered is a file manager in the terminal. So I can just look through that, or I can open it up in Zed, which is what I use now, just to view markdown files, edit them. If it's a changelog, for example, I want to tweak something briefly, go back to the CLI, and then just let it rip from there. And any tool or feature I think I'm missing, I'll have a crack at building it myself—like a terminal file viewer."
[ 24m53s538ms - 24m58s998ms ] The screen returns to the man speaking. He is giving a final message.

summarization.content: The speaker discusses a Tweet by Ben Tossell which details how it's possible to code with AI agents without being technical.  He highlights several key points from the article, including shipping quality products, using a CLI, and working on Github repos. He concludes that while coding has a lot of options, the more you use code and AI-related tools, the better you will become.

So why—if an LLM is super smart—why couldn't it just be simpler code written, less dependencies, less potential surface areas for bugs? Is that a silly thought or a good thought? And I can learn that it might not be a silly thought. But okay, yes, there are these many projects that the model has been trained on, which is why often things will be built in certain frameworks. So it's just building up this understanding of the code world, the engineering world that I didn't deserve to be in, but I'm absolutely part of now. Beyond "vibe coding" Yes, you can call it vibe coding, but I think vibe coding misses the point. I'm trying to actually learn the systems. I'm trying to really understand what is going on, how can I improve, how can I be a new age programmer, what is this new technical class? That's what I think is the most interesting thing here. I can't categorically call myself non-technical but I also can't call myself a programmer. Nor would I want to. "I'm part of this new technical class and I don't know what it's called." But I think vibe coding gives a negative connotation to it, much like no-code gave a negative connotation to that group. It feels like a game Some people have likened this new way of programming to a game. Factorio is the one that people talk about. I've never played it. I'm not much of a gamer. But this whole paradigm feels like a real game to me, and the output is I'm building stuff that I want to build. A ton of things just don't end up anywhere on Github. They don't end up live. They are just mere explorations of parts of a system or a topic. Others end up published and other people use it - I had a CTO fork my personal site and use it for himself! Big boss stuff (for me!) If someone posts "oh, I built this React grab tool for example". Okay, cool, can I build my own? Like why? This one looks really good. Well, just because I want to. I can just explore things for the sake of exploring things. "Every idea you've ever had can be exercised, can be explored, and it doesn't need to be good" And you'll learn along the way. Permission to throw things away Previously, if I'd learnt to code to build a really crappy version of something I was thinking of, like a big idea that I had, and then no one wanted it, I'd be too emotionally invested in that idea to be able to just throw it away. With no-code, I could effectively build a version of that big idea in an hour, a couple of hours, a weekend. And if no one liked it, no one wanted to pay for it, it was rubbish, then I could just throw it away. It wasn't that much of my time or my energy into something that ultimately wasn't going to be something good for someone else. And I feel like the same is true today. We're gonna see an explosion of software. Many of it won't be good, but lots of it is already great. There are expert programmers who are shipping things like absolute crazy that are all good projects. So we're just gonna have this absolute plethora of coded projects out there that you can use, clone, tweak, remix. It'll take a lot less time than if you had to learn to code or if you're reading the files or you're writing the files or anything like that. It's just a lot quicker. The feedback loop is quicker. The process is quicker. You can just do anything at any time and just consistently keep churning out stuff. Fail forward The way to learn about code is to build ahead of your capability and fail forward. I feel like everyone who is not technical today who wants to be in this world, who wants to do stuff like this, can absolutely do it. They just need some permission to do that. To play around. You must think of it like play. Sign up to a CLI agent like Droid. Say you want to build a personal website. Say you want to build a little RSS feed tracker, a little to-do list, a little workout app. Whatever you want to do, you just spin it up, start working on it. Every little hiccup, bug, or issue you run into—question it. Okay, why did this come up? Why did you hit those errors? You know you don't know how to code, so you shouldn't get bogged down with bugs—expert programmers hit bugs all the time. And you can take it to other places. You can go to ChatGPT or Claude and give it to different models for different perspectives. You're always gonna have all of the choice up there and all the different variations. Just pick one There are just so many different tools, so many different options. Ultimately, just pick one and just stick with it. Just learn that system. They all look fairly similar. They all work similarly. Obviously, I use Droid because I work at Factory. But also they get the best output of any models. (yay for model agnostic) Ultimately, what I want and what I need from a tool is: 'Is this one gonna help me get the furthest I can in the least amount of time with the least amount of trouble?' The more I have to do with using the tools themselves, the harder it is. Things like IDEs—I've tried a bunch. I used to use one in particular for a long time. It's just got so much extra stuff that I just don't need or care about. I just want to talk to a model, have code written. If I need to inspect some markdown files, I can now use what I've just recently discovered is a file manager in the terminal. So I can just look through that, or I can open it up in Zed, which is what I use now, just to view markdown files, edit them. If it's a changelog, for example, I want to tweak something briefly, go back to the CLI, and then just let it rip from there. And any tool or feature I think I'm missing, I'll have a crack at building it myself—like a terminal file viewer. "This whole thing is just a really big learning experience for me, and I'm really enjoying it. Build, fail forward, and keep shipping." (20:25-29:30)

At 21:49, the video shows a brief glimpse of the speaker's Twitter profile, including a recent post (21:50-22:25).

The video concludes with the speaker again directly addressing the camera, offering advice and encouraging viewers (29:53-30:20).

Tossell shares that he has contributed simple improvements to his company's products. He learns by observing engineers, watching their Pull Requests (PRs), and participating in internal lunches where discussions cover product features and bug fixes. **17:07 - 18:07: Why This is Different**

Now, he approaches it from a systems thinking perspective, understanding how tools like Webflow, Zapier, and Airtable form the "front end," "API routes," "connective tissue," and "database" of a system. **18:07 - 20:24: No Piece of Software Feels Unattainable**

**20:24 - 21:44: Asking the "Silly" Questions**
He encourages asking "silly questions" that other programmers might shy away from. With AI, there's "no one watching me and no one shooting me down for being stupid or saying the wrong thing." He questions why frameworks are used when an LLM could potentially generate simpler code with fewer dependencies and bugs. He believes this is not a silly thought but a valid inquiry, as models are trained on these frameworks. This process builds understanding of the code world.

**21:44 - 22:54: Beyond "Vibe Coding"**
Tossell prefers to call his process "learning the systems" rather than "vibe coding." He sees himself as part of a "new technical class" that focuses on understanding, improving, and mastering this programmable layer of abstraction. He likens this new way of programming to a game, where the output is building stuff you want to build. He sees many things built as explorations, not necessarily for production, and finds joy in this.

**22:54 - 29:28: Fail Forward & Just Pick One**

The more you have to manually do with a tool, the harder it is.
* **IDEs:** He finds Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) often contain "so much extra stuff" that he doesn't need. He prefers talking to a model, having code written, and then using a file manager in the terminal or Zed (his editor) to inspect and edit markdown files or tweak changes. If he's missing a tool or feature, he'll build it himself (like a terminal file viewer).

**29:28 - 30:20: Conclusion**
The speaker reiterates Ben Tossell's final message: "This whole thing is just a really big learning experience for me, and I'm really enjoying it. Build, fail forward, and keep shipping." He encourages viewers to commit to this process, build things in 2026, and share their ideas.
